newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists seen selling off financial firms.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists seen selling off financial firms.

text.p: The new French Socialist government is sending strong signals it will start selling state firms, rowing back on the party's anti-privatisation election talk, and the financial sector is expected to be targeted.

In his clearest statement so far on selloffs, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin promised late last week to look at privatisation case-by-case, saying he would seek the best solutions and be guided by national interest, not ideology.
"It's clear Jospin wants to get rid of all those firms nationalised at the start of the Socialist era (in the 1980s)," said Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney.
He believes the government will eventually privatise insurer GAN and its regional banking subsidiary CIC, and bank Credit Lyonnais, among other companies.
Underlying the pragmatism is a wish to unload companies which have cost the state billions of francs in handouts.
"I'm not sure it's the state's role to keep on bailing out financial institutions in trouble," Jospin said last week.
The government also needs money from the sale of profitable state firms to prop up ailing ones without worsening the budget deficit as it seeks to qualify for European monetary union.
The previous conservative government had targeted a host of state-owned companies for sale but those plans were put on hold by the Socialists when they were elected on June 1.
The sale of a minority stake in France Telecom was expected to generate a vital 30 billion francs to 50 billion francs ($5-$8.5 billion) for state coffers.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has already indicated that this sale will go ahead, declaring last month he was not against its privatisation as long as staff were consulted.
GAN, CIC and Credit Lyonnais, along with a smaller regional bank, Societe Marseillaise, had also been targeted for privatisation by the conservative administration.
GAN, whose troubles stem from disastrous diversification and huge losses at its property unit UIC, has received 2.8 billion francs in state funds and is due to get 20 billion more.

The government is negotiating with the European Commission on the rescue of GAN. To win Commission backing for the injection of funds, the government is expected to go ahead with privatisation of the insurer.

The most likely scenario calls for a merger between GAN and rival AGF through a share swap, press reports say. AGF has expressed interest in GAN following the megamerger between insurers Axa and UAP. But there are potential foreign suitors -- Germany's Allianz ALVD.F and Belgium's Fortis.

The conservative government had said it could privatise Credit Lyonnais this year. The bank nearly collapsed in the early 1990s after an ill-fated expansion spree, expected to cost taxpayers up to 170 billion francs over a period of years.
Stripped by a 1995 state rescue of its bad assets, it is recovering strongly but the Socialists are expected to wait until its recovery is cemented before putting it up for sale.

A rescue plan for the bank calls for the state to neutralise the impact of a loan that Credit Lyonnais was forced to extend under the 1995 bailout. The loan to the state agency which took over Credit Lyonnais's dud assets threatens to put the bank back into the red.
The Commission is expected to insist on privatisation to approve the move. The sale could initially be in the form of opening part of its capital to private investors late next year, reports say.

Press reports say Societe Marseillaise de Credit which has cost the state 2.9 billion francs in the past four years and will need 300 to 400 million francs more, is also expected to be sold in exchange for Commission approval of aid.
Jospin's pledge to be "flexible" on privatisation have fired hopes that defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF would also be privatised and even flag carrier Air France. ($ = 5.891 French Francs)
